coach_says: The knight on e4 was attacking your bishop on c3, and castling ignored it. Black simply took on c3 and, with the bishop gone and ...Bg4 pinning your f3 knight, your extra pawn on e5 fell. Instead, take the attacker: Bxe4 dxe4 leaves the e4 pawn loose in front of your queen, so you win it and go two pawns up. When an enemy piece lands in your camp attacking something, first ask whether you can capture it.

Your bishop on c4 was attacked by the knight on d6, and Ng5 didn't do anything about it. The attack on f7 isn't a threat either, because that same d6 knight guards f7. Black just took the bishop with ...Nxc4. Move the bishop first (Bb3), then Re1 and Nxe5 win back your pawn. Before starting an attack, check whether any of your pieces are hanging.

Your rook on a8 was attacked, and Bb7 saved it but let White swap bishops and castle into safety. Rd8 saves the rook with a threat: it pins the d5 bishop to White's queen on d1, and with Nf6 also hitting d5, White has to spend time defending (Qf3) while their king is still in the middle. When a piece is attacked, look for a move that saves it and creates a threat of its own, especially along an open file pointing at the enemy queen.
also: keep the enemy king in the centre

coach_says: After Nh6+ White plays Kh5 and the king attacks both your knights at once, because the knights on g6 and h6 don't protect each other. Saving one with ...Ng8 then lets Rd4+ drive your king away from the e4 bishop, so you lose a piece anyway. Ne5+ keeps your knights together in the centre near your own king. In endgames, keep your minor pieces protecting each other and away from the enemy king.

Qc7 looks active, hitting b7 and d8, but ...R2d7 covers both, and then your queen has to run back to g3 while Black's rooks gain time. Meanwhile your bishop on a7 is still out of play. Bd4 was better: it brings the bishop back into the game, blocks the d-file and attacks the f6 knight. When your queen raids the far side, check whether one simple move stops everything and leaves you just losing time.

After d4 Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Qxd4, Black plays ...c5 hitting your queen and then ...c4 attacking your b3 bishop. This is the Noah's Ark trap: the bishop can only hide on a2, where it is buried behind Black's pawns, and your e4 pawn gets weak. With the bishop on b3 and Black's pawns on a6 and b5, be careful about opening the centre; d3 keeps things solid.

f6 doesn't develop anything, takes the best square away from your g8 knight and opens the diagonal towards your king. It also makes castling kingside riskier and leaves e6 weak. In the opening, develop pieces first: Nf6, Bf5 or e6 all do something useful. Only move the f-pawn when there's a clear reason.

Taking on f7 was right, but with the rook, not the bishop. Rxf7 puts your rook on the seventh rank, where it eats g7 next and ties Black's knight and h8 rook down, with ideas like Bg5+ to follow. Bxf7 just wins the pawn and the bishop gets chased by ...Ke7. When you can capture with a rook to reach the seventh rank, that is usually the stronger recapture.

Your bishop on e6 was shielding your king on the e-file. When it went to grab a2, White played Re2 and pinned your e5 knight to your king. The bishop is also stuck on a2, where b3 can shut it out of the game. You are winning, so keep your pieces working together: Bd7 keeps the bishop near the action and avoids the pin.

You're a piece down, so you need moves that build something. Qb3+ is a check, but after ...Kg7 your queen has nothing to do and later goes back to d1. b4 instead gains space with tempo on the c5 bishop and lets your knight jump to c4. A check is only worth playing if it improves your position or leads to something.

g6 leaves holes on the dark squares around your king, especially f6 and h6. White answers Bg5, pinning your e7 knight, and later Bf6 lands right in the hole. Ng6 was simpler: it gets the knight out of the way so your f8 bishop can develop and keeps your pawns intact. Before pushing a pawn in front of your king, check which squares it stops guarding.

Your queen was attacked, and the best way out was Qxf3: f3 was attacked by your queen and the h5 bishop and only defended by White's queen, so after Qxf3 Qxf3 Bxf3 you win another pawn and trade queens. Qg6 lets White put a rook on the open g-file with Rg1, gaining time, and your d6 pawn is left loose. When your queen has to move, look for a square where it captures something, and when you're ahead, trading queens is good news.

White's two knights were both hitting f6, which only the g7 pawn defended. After Nb4, White plays Ndxf6+ gxf6 Nxf6+ and wins two pawns while your king is stuck in the middle with no shelter. Nxd5 removes one of the attackers and the threat disappears. Before starting your own play, count attackers and defenders on the squares near your king.

Bh5+ is a check, but after ...Kd8 Black's king is quite safe in this closed position and your bishop is offside on h5. You still have to deal with ...g5, which hits your f4 bishop and boxes in your h3 knight. Bg3 deals with that first and keeps your pieces flexible. Don't give a check just because you can; ask what the piece does on its new square.

Both black knights were loose on g6 and h6, and Kh5 attacks the two of them at once with no knight check available to save them. Kg5 also attacks both, but it walks onto a square where ...Nf7+ comes with check, so Black saves a knight with tempo. After Kh5 Ng8, Rd4+ also drives the king away from the e4 bishop and you win it. When your king forks pieces, pick the square where the enemy has no check to escape with.

Good move. Bxg7 wins a pawn and goes after the h8 rook. Black can take on f1 with the d2 knight, but you collect the rook and stay completely winning. Just keep an eye on loose pieces as you grab material.
Good move. Ne4 hits the queen and the d6 bishop, and trading off that bishop leaves Black's king stuck in the centre with your rook coming to e1. That's exactly the right plan.

You are well ahead in material and g6 keeps you winning. Qf6 was a bit sharper, going after the c3 square and the c1 bishop, but the difference doesn't matter much here. Keep trading down and finishing the game.
Fine. Your king keeps an eye on the h2 knight and your g7 pawn is about to win the game; Kg2, Kg3 and Kf2 all work.
You're already losing here, and Qf6 is about as good as anything else. The real problem came earlier; now just keep your pieces active and hope for chances.
